title: How Active Directory Ties Windows Server Together

scenes.line1: What's the backbone of a Windows domain?
scenes.line2: Why does everything need Active Directory?
scenes.say: What's the backbone of a Windows domain? Why does everything need Active Directory?

scenes.label: AD
scenes.sub: Active Directory stores users, computers, and groups.
scenes.say: Active Directory is the directory for users, computers, and groups. It's the core of Windows Server domains.

scenes.label: DC
scenes.sub: Domain controllers authenticate and replicate changes.
scenes.say: Domain controllers authenticate logins and replicate changes to each other, so every login checks with Active Directory.

rows.b: Clients find them via SRV records

scenes.say: Active Directory depends on DNS. Domain controllers register special records, so clients can find them. If DNS breaks, logins and Group Policy stop working.

scenes.title: Forcing Group Policy
scenes.say: When Group Policy isn't applying, use gpupdate slash force to refresh, and gpresult slash r to see what applied.

scenes.code:
Get-ADUser -Filter *
Get-EventLog -LogName System
Get-Process | Sort CPU -desc
scenes.say: PowerShell is the admin shell. Use commands like Get AD User, Get Event Log, and Get Process to manage and troubleshoot.

scenes.question: Can you link a GPO to a security group?
scenes.right: No. GPOs link to OUs, not groups. Groups grant permissions.
scenes.say: Here's a classic trap: Can you link a Group Policy Object to a security group? No—you link GPOs to Organizational Units, not groups. Groups are for permissions.
